speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment whether the National Environment Agency will review the practice of operators of Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centres requiring hawkers to absorb the 10% discount offered to customers paying via the operator apps.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: My response to this Parliamentary Question (PQ) will also cover questions filed by Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Abdul Muhaimin Abdul Malik, Mr Ng Shi Xuan1 and Ms He Ting Ru regarding Socially-conscious Enterprise Hawker Centres (SEHCs).

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: If their questions have been addressed in today's combined response, they may wish to withdraw their questions.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I will explain the SEHC management model and address various concerns, including the Government's role in overseeing SEHC operators and their relationship with stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: When the Government resumed building hawker centres in 2011, we introduced the SEHC.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This is to harness the experience and expertise of food and beverage (F&B) industry players to bring fresh perspectives and best practices to hawker centre management, active placemaking and meeting residents' needs for accessibility to affordable food options across all three meals.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The National Environment Agency (NEA) maintains oversight over operators who are appointed to maintain and manage SEHCs.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Operators must comply with the requirements set out by NEA.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: These requirements strike a balance between ensuring that patrons' needs are adequately served and safeguarding stallholders' well-being.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: NEA also seeks to provide SEHC operators with sufficient flexibility to allow them to operate SEHCs effectively.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: For instance, stalls should not be required to be open for more than five days per week and no more than eight hours a day, and limits are set on amounts that operators can charge stallholders for contractual breaches.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The key features of NEA's guidelines had been made public during the Parliamentary debates in 2018 and 2024.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Before stallholders sign these tenancy agreements with an operator, NEA would review the agreements and engage operators to adjust their clauses if necessary.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Beyond these guidelines, operators have the flexibility to state the other terms of their agreements with stallholders, based on operational needs.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: However, these terms must be made upfront by operators, so that hawkers can make informed decisions based on their business preferences and cost considerations.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Operators must also explain these terms clearly to stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: NEA officers would usually be present at these tenancy agreements signing sessions.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: After tenancy agreements are signed, operators must not impose any charges that were not specified in the agreements.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: As tenancy agreements are private arrangements between the operators and stallholders, it would not be appropriate for NEA to mandate public disclosure.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Some Members have asked about affordable meal options.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: In line with the primary mission of hawker centres to provide affordable food options, NEA requires SEHC operators, as part of tender requirements, to implement ways to make food affordable.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So far, SEHC operators have done so by making at least one value meal available at each stall.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Value meals are part of the range of food options afforded by the SEHCs at variety price points.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: SEHC operators explain the value meal requirement upfront to stallholders when signing the tenancy agreements.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Each stallholder then has the flexibility to propose his or her value meal item, while retaining the prerogative to offer other food options at higher prices.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This takes into account their costs and pricing strategies.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Operators will also review their value meal prices from time to time and have previously adjusted prices upwards based on feedback from stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Importantly, stallholders are not expected to make a loss from selling such value meals as they should have taken these into consideration when negotiating the rent with the operators.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Some Members have also asked about charitable meal schemes.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So far, only Bukit Canberra Hawker Centre has such a scheme.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The operator's Pay-It-Forward initiative was a well-intentioned initiative to give lower-income members of our community some additional support as part of our shared interest to make the hawker centre an inclusive community dining option.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The scheme was made known to stallholders upfront before they decided whether to rent stalls at this particular SEHC.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Therefore, stallholders who decided to proceed with renting stalls at the centre, rather than choose other centres without such a scheme, would have factored the costs into their business consideration.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Some operators have developed phone apps which offer discounts to loyal customers.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This is among various initiatives introduced by operators to attract patrons, increase footfall and encourage repeat customers at their SEHCs, which would also benefit stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: SEHC operators bear the costs of developing such apps and conducting marketing and publicity efforts, while stallholders bear a portion of the costs by providing discounts in return for increased sales.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This is an example of the partnership and shared efforts of operators and stallholders to make their SEHCs vibrant and successful.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This serves as a regular platform for stallholders to provide feedback or ideas on improving the operations of SEHCs, or raise any areas of concern.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: For example, one operator took in feedback about high gas costs and will explore lower cost options after the current gas contract expires.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Another operator stepped up checks on the segregation of trays and crockery following feedback from stallholders as well.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This consultative approach between operators and stallholders fosters trust and understanding and allows differences to be addressed and SEHC operations to be improved.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Nevertheless, we always welcome and have heard your feedback.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Moving forward, we will continue to improve the SEHC management model through constructive engagement with stakeholders and continuous refinements to better serve the interests of our community.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The first, how do the average independently assessed value rents, which the SEHCs rentals are kept at, compare against that of NEA's own-managed hawker centres?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second, while the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has mentioned the intent is that stallholders are not expected to make losses from selling the value meals, has NEA conducted a survey to understand if that is how indeed all hawkers understand the policy intent and have implemented it in such a way?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I ask because I would expect there to be a wide variation in the practices on the ground, because there are some food types like "cai png" or economy rice, where this would be much more easily implementable as compared to say, Japanese food, where the base of the food cost is already higher.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My third clarification is, I understand that the discounts that the operators have on their apps for loyal customers can benefit the stallholders, but I would argue that they certainly would benefit the operators as much, if not more.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, my question is, does NEA know the proportion of the costs being borne by both sides?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is it the operators that bear the bulk of the cost, or is it the hawkers?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would argue that the operators should bear the bulk of the cost, because if indeed, it is for attracting footfall to the hawkers, then we can leave it to the hawkers themselves to implement their own discounts, rather than having one centralised and imposed on them.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: For the first question, the Member asked about the average independently valued rents at the SEHCs, how do they compare with that at NEA-managed hawker centres?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: However, I would also like to highlight that when we compare rent, it should also not debase on absolute rent because we have to consider stall sizes and amenities in the centre.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Those who have been to SEHCs would recognise that the stall sizes there are slightly bigger and also, there are other amenities that the stallholders would benefit from.
The second question that the Member asked was about whether NEA has conducted a survey to understand how hawkers have understood the requirements and implemented the value meal requirement.

To talk the Member through the process of how hawkers are made aware and how they implement the value meal requirement: first, these terms are made clear upfront by the operators prior to signing the tenancy agreements with the stallholders and they are required to then explain the terms clearly to the stallholders.
So, the stallholders walk in with their eyes wide open about what is required and what they need to provide for the value meals.
Operators then work closely with the stallholders on the provision of these value meals, so that they can determine what to sell for these value meals.
The price is given and the stallholders then have the flexibility to put together a range of ingredients to meet that price.
And that is not the end of story.
From time to time, we understand that prices would increase with inflation and other reasons.
Operators have also then reviewed these value meal prices and adjusted accordingly based on feedback from the stallholders.
So, I would say that it is an ongoing process and the stallholders are continuously engaged to ensure that they understand and implement these value meal requirements properly.

For the last question that the Member raised about the proportionate contribution between stallholders as well as the operators, I am glad that the Member has also pointed out that a loyalty programme pretty much benefits all parties in this situation.
It benefits the stallholders because of increased footfall.
Operators tend to gain as well and, of course, patrons tend to benefit from these discounts.
The discounts are then born by stallholders at the stall level.
And this will help to attract returning customers.
So, in all the cases that we have seen across SEHCs that have operated such programmes, the operators are the ones that develop and maintain these apps and publicity efforts.
These are done and extracted from the 50% of operating surplus that we require SEHC operators to plough back into the centre.

I would also like to highlight that beyond developing these apps, there are other ways that our operators have also driven traffic to centres, which, I think, we can agree could be very costly undertakings, such as shuttle buses, organising festive events, fringe events and so on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Two supplementary questions for the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is in relation to the "Pay It Forward" free meals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Can I understand if NEA was aware of the contractual obligation of this, especially given that the operators would also have explained this to the hawkers themselves?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And given, I think, what Senior Parliamentary Secretary said just now about how hawkers are not supposed to be making losses on these charitable initiatives, does NEA now take the view that these should not actually be part of the SEHC operator contractual agreements, and that these will be also included in the NEA guidelines going forward?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to the part on my original PQ, in terms of whether the Ministry will review the current distribution of responsibility for the provision of affordable and free meals, given that now it seems to have befallen squarely on the hawkers themselves?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I will answer the first part of the first question squarely, and then I will combine my answer to the first and the second question.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: To explain, for tenancy agreements, NEA has specific guidelines that were shared in previous Parliamentary debates.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I mentioned examples of working hours as well as liquidated damages and a cap to those amounts.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Beyond these hard guidelines, NEA does provide flexibility for operators to then commercially decide, together with the stallholders, on what might be the most appropriate other conditions to build in that recognise location and centre-specific differences.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So, it will safeguard a certain set of guidelines; and for everything else, there is flexibility for operators to decide on that to stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: What is important to us is that these are made clear and agreed upon with stallholders when tenancy agreements are signed.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Because that is where stallholders should also have the responsibility and the ability, frankly, to then agree to these things, calculate it as part as their business decisions when deciding to locate their business in the SEHC versus other SEHCs or NEA hawker centres.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The point about charitable initiatives and hawkers not expecting to make a loss, I would like to first differentiate.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: There are the value meal requirements, which are your lower-cost items, generally between $3.00 and $3.50 per meal, versus the "Pay It Forward" initiative.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: For the value meal requirement, that is where we say that hawkers are not expected to make a loss.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I give you a price, $3.00 to $3.50, and then you figure out how to meet that within the cost of your ingredients so that you are not making a loss.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So, my comment was related to the first concept.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The second concept on "Pay It Forward", because the stallholders then discuss that together with the operator, it is within the stallholders' consideration set as well, how they will then meet that.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: If they say they are able to, that is their business decision.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: And I assume that accounts for their pricing and their marketing strategies as well.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I thought to make it very clear that these are two very different concepts.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: To the Member's question about the distribution of responsibilities for providing low-cost nutrition meals and whether that is entirely fallen on the hawker itself and whether we should review the spread of responsibility.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I think we should recognise that the value meal requirement, firstly, again to reiterate, that hawkers are not expected to make a loss.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So, the hawker themselves, this is not expected to result in any business losses.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: This should also then be seen in the context of what the other parties in the system are supporting hawkers with as well.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: And now, the Government steps in as well: the cost of constructing and maintaining a hawker centre, we all know it is in the millions, and that is something that the Government does not recover from the operator and the stallholders.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: So, in fact, there is the value meal requirement, but there is also the context in which we are supporting hawkers that we should also recognise that other parties have provided support for our hawkers too.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does NEA have the power to veto specific clauses, specifically those regarding the turnover-based rent, mandatory supplier use or punitive fees?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, I want to come back to the point that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has addressed just now about the value meals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary said that the hawkers are not expected to make a loss selling the value meals, and the Senior Parliamentary Secretary went on to say that the provision of the value meals is a shared responsibility and pointed out the Government already heavily subsidises the construction and running of the hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, given that hawkers are often low-income earners, why should individual hawkers have to bear any of the cost of a social programme, like the provision of a value meal?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Should the cost of this not be socialised?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The Member's first question was about contract signing and whether NEA has any veto rights within the contract signing process.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: NEA would step in: one, I mentioned earlier on when the guidelines that we put out, the few guidelines that we think are "no-nos", we will step in if those are being infringed.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: And the other point that we may come in is when we believe that some of the conditions might be too one-sided or overly legalistic.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: In certain cases when we see that there may be hidden costs, we would then step in.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Certainly, there is space for us to come in to do that, but more often than not, I think it is reasonable for us to leave some flexibility because the stallholders are there, and if it is understood and it is clearly explained to them, then the conditions and terms would be inside the contract.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: The other question is why should hawkers have to bear any of the cost?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: I suppose my question back is what is the cost that the Member is referring to?

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: Over here, we are saying that value meal items, it should be a price point and then the hawkers themselves would sell a meal that is at that price point, within a suite of food options that could be at different prices.

speaker: Ms Goh Hanyan
text: And so, the cost, in this case, is not as direct as the Member has said, in terms of us forcing the hawker to provide a certain subsidy upfront.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Moving on to the next lot of questions.
